newsitem.title: USA: WHX, steelworkers continue talks on Friday.
newsitem.headline: WHX, steelworkers continue talks on Friday.

text.p: Contract talks between WHX Corp and the United Steelworkers union resumed on Friday after ending abruptly on Thursday.

"The company came in (Thursday) and said here's our offer, if you don't accept it, that's the end of talks," an angry Jim Bowen, the union's chief negotiator, said at a news conference early Friday before talks resumed.

Bowen said company negotiators walked away from the bargaining table Thursday. The company, in a statement issued late Thursday, said the union had rejected a proposal offering pension improvements and other benefits.
Some 4,700 steelworkers have been on strike at WHX since October 1. The strike has idled eight steel plants in three states. WHX already warned it will post a fourth-quarter loss due to the strike.
The two sides are at an impasse that some industry sources say is unsolvable unless one side gives in to the other.
The union wants WHX to establish a defined benefit pension plan, under which contributions are guaranteed and based on wages and length of service.
WHX has steadfastly maintained it cannot afford such a plan and says that type of plan helped force it into bankruptcy 11 years ago.

Instead, WHX has offered to enhance its defined contribution plan, under which a percentage of a worker's pay is contributed to an investment fund, and benefits that are paid out depend on how the fund performs.

Bowen blasted the company's offer made on Thursday, which included an offer of unreduced pension benefits at age 60 instead of 62. "That slight improvement does nothing to address the major concern...which is to have pensions that are both adequate and secure."

The company also offered that retirees will be eligible for $1,600-per-month pensions after 42 years of service instead of 44 years. "To require 42 years of hard labor for such a pension is hardly generous," Bowen said.
Bowen said the union has $180 million in its strike fund to distribute to workers. "That fund will not dry up...we can go on with this strike one day longer than the company can handle."
